title: Water from the Rock and the Deaths of Miriam and Aaron
summary: Miriam dies at Kadesh, and when the people quarrel with Moses over lack of water, God tells Moses to speak to the rock. Instead Moses rebukes the people and strikes the rock twice; water flows, but God tells Moses and Aaron that because they did not trust him to show his holiness, they will not bring Israel into the land. Edom refuses Israel passage along the King's Highway, and at Mount Hor Aaron's priestly garments are placed on his son Eleazar before Aaron dies.
story: Numbers 20 marks a turning point. The long years of wandering are ending, and the old generation is passing away, beginning with its leaders. Miriam, the sister who watched over the infant Moses and led Israel's song at the sea (Exodus 15:20-21), dies at the start of the chapter; Aaron, the first high priest, dies at its end. Between these deaths Moses himself falls, at the very spring where the people fall once again into complaint. By the end of the chapter it is certain that none of the three siblings who led Israel out of Egypt will lead it into Canaan. The story now turns toward the plains of Moab and the new generation, and the route to the land will have to go around Edom rather than through it.
historical:
The chapter's first verse gives the first month but not the year. Comparing it with Numbers 33:38, which dates Aaron's death to the fortieth year after the exodus, most interpreters conclude that this is the fortieth year, so that almost four decades of wilderness life pass silently between chapters 19 and 20. Others think the arrival at Kadesh refers to an earlier stay there. Kadesh, also called Kadesh Barnea, lay on the southern edge of Canaan; it is often identified with a site in the northeastern Sinai with good springs, though the identification is not certain. The location of Mount Hor is also debated. A long tradition places it near Petra in modern Jordan, but many scholars look for it closer to Kadesh, since verse 23 locates it on the border of Edom.

Edom lay south and southeast of the Dead Sea, and its people were understood as descendants of Esau, Jacob's brother (Genesis 36), which is why Moses' message calls Israel “your brother”. The King's Highway was the main north and south route through the highlands east of the Jordan. How organized Edom was in the period of the exodus is debated by historians and archaeologists, since much of the evidence for a developed Edomite kingdom comes from later centuries, but Egyptian texts from the late second millennium BC already mention the people of Edom.
cultural:
Water was life in the wilderness. Springs and wells were jealously guarded, and in a dry land water belonged to whoever controlled the source, which is why Israel offers to pay for any water its herds drink (verse 19). A request to pass through another people's territory on a main road, promising not to cut through fields or vineyards, was a normal diplomatic approach, and Moses' message follows the pattern of such letters: the sender's identity, a recital of history, the request, and assurances. Edom's refusal and its show of force are an insult between brothers that later prophets did not forget (see Obadiah).

The transfer of Aaron's garments to Eleazar (verses 26 to 28) was a visible succession. The high priest's vestments were described in detail in Exodus 28, and wearing them was what marked the office. By stripping them from Aaron and clothing Eleazar before Aaron died, Moses made clear that the priesthood did not die with its first holder. Israel's thirty days of mourning for Aaron matches the mourning later given to Moses himself (Deuteronomy 34:8), a sign of the honor in which he was held.
literary: The chapter has three episodes framed by two deaths: Miriam (verse 1), the waters of Meribah (2 to 13), Edom's refusal (14 to 21), and Aaron's death (22 to 29). The Meribah story deliberately echoes Exodus 17:1-7, an earlier water crisis at a place also called Meribah, where God told Moses to strike the rock. Here the command is different: take the staff, but speak to the rock. The wordplay in verse 13 ties the place name Meribah to the verb quarreled (riv) and the holiness God shows to the name Kadesh, which comes from the root for holy. The chapter's verbs of rebellion (verses 10 and 24) cut both ways: Moses calls the people rebels, and then God says Moses and Aaron rebelled.

outline.t: The waters of Meribah and the sin of Moses and Aaron
Aaron dies on Mount Hor and Eleazar succeeds him

doctrines.note: God's complaint is that Moses and Aaron did not treat him as holy before the people (verse 12). Leaders who handle holy things are held to a high standard, and God still shows his holiness by providing water and by judging his servants.
The charge is literally that they did not believe or trust God. Faith here is not only belief that God can act but obedience to how he says he will act.
Even in the midst of the leaders' failure, water gushes out for the whole congregation and their animals. God's provision for his people is not canceled by the failures of those who lead them.

words.note: Meribah, meaning quarreling or contention. The name recalls the earlier crisis in Exodus 17 and becomes shorthand in later Scripture for Israel's testing of God in the wilderness (Psalm 95:8; Psalm 106:32). Here it also becomes the place where Moses and Aaron lost their entrance to the land.

Sela, crag or rock, a high cliff or rock face. Exodus 17 uses a different word (tsur) for the rock Moses struck. Some interpreters see the change of word as a sign that this is a new event with a new command, while others think the two words are used almost interchangeably.

Qadash, to be holy or to treat as holy. God says that Moses and Aaron did not trust him to show his holiness, and verse 13 says that God showed his holiness among them anyway. The play on the place name Kadesh makes the lesson hard to miss.
Marah, to rebel or be defiant. Moses calls the people rebels in verse 10, and in verse 24 God uses the same verb for what Moses and Aaron did. The accuser is found guilty of the same thing.

christ: Paul says that in the wilderness Israel drank from a spiritual rock that followed them, and that the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). He means that the one who provided water in the desert was present with Israel and is known now as Christ, not that every detail of the rock is a symbol. Many Christian interpreters have added that the rock, once struck in Exodus 17, did not need to be struck again, and some see in that an echo of Christ's once-for-all death (Hebrews 9:28); this is a later reflection rather than something the text states. The death of Aaron also points forward in a way the New Testament makes explicit: the Levitical priests were many because death kept them from continuing, but Jesus holds his priesthood permanently because he lives forever (Hebrews 7:23-25). Aaron's garments had to pass to another; Christ's priesthood never does.

hard.q: What exactly did Moses do wrong, and why was the punishment so severe?
hard.a:
The text does not spell it out, and interpreters give several answers, often combining them. Some focus on the act: God said speak to the rock, and Moses struck it twice, reverting to the method of Exodus 17 rather than obeying the new command. Others focus on the words: Moses said “must we bring you water out of this rock”, as if he and Aaron were the source, and Psalm 106:32-33 remembers that he spoke rashly. Others stress the anger: calling God's people rebels misrepresented a God who was about to give water without a word of rebuke. God's own verdict names the root: they did not trust him, and so did not honor him as holy before the people.

The severity fits the principle that leaders are judged more strictly because their actions shape how a whole people sees God. The judgment was also mixed with mercy. Moses remained Israel's leader, would see the land from Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34), and appears with Jesus in the land at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3), which some readers find a fitting end to his story. The chapter does not soften the loss, but it does not cast him away either.

questions: Moses did the right thing for decades and then failed in a moment of exhaustion and anger. What pressures make you most likely to misrepresent God to others?
Water came out of the rock even though Moses disobeyed. How do you hold together God's faithfulness to his people and his seriousness about the failures of their leaders?
Aaron's garments passed to Eleazar before Aaron died. What would it look like for you to hand on what you have been given before you have to?
